Tech stocks aren't lacking in growth stories for 2027. The problem is that smart money is increasingly selective about which companies it's willing to pay a premium for. AI is still the big story, but skepticism is growing about whether the money invested will deliver the promised returns.

You could see that shift very clearly in the Bank of America fund manager survey for November. Investors were clearly pulling back from tech at the fastest rate since June 2006 (their net overweight position in tech fell from 37% in October to just 12%). Even more telling is that 38% of the 169 managers surveyed (who in total manage $461 billion) believe that firms are over-investing in AI and over half (52%) expect at least one of the major AI players to reduce its capital expenditure over the next 6 months.

The concerns led to a wider sell-off. The Nasdaq 100 Index is down over 10% in the second half of 2026. Semiconductors were particularly hard hit as investors have re-priced AI companies and rethought the sustainability of data center spending. This wasn't necessarily a rejection of AI per se. It was more a case of investors questioning how much expected growth had already been priced in.

There's still a lot of money flowing into the sector. JPMorgan expects AI-related capex to be $1.4tn in 2027, almost double its 2026 estimate. A significant portion will go into data centers, servers, networking gear and advanced semiconductors. For a closer look at where this spending is going, see our breakdown of the eight companies Morgan Stanley expects to spend $1.6 trillion on AI infrastructure in 2027. JPMorgan does, however, expect spending growth to tail off significantly from 2028.

The wider tech sector isn't moving in the same direction. Chip and data center suppliers are clearly on the up because of AI spending. On the other hand, the software and cloud businesses have to prove that their customers are actually going to spend more. For investors, it's all about separating the wheat from the chaff. Some businesses have sustainable demand while others are just in the midst of a spending spike.

The search for value is also playing out across the broader market. In a recent article, we look at 10 dirt-cheap stocks positioned to soar in 2027, focusing on companies that trade at attractive valuations despite strong expected revenue growth.

So, what are the best tech stocks to buy for 2027? You can find the expanded list of 10 Best Tech Stocks to Buy for 2027 According to Hedge Funds. We discussed the top 5 stocks below.

title: Jensen Huang Is Back. Nvidia’s (NVDA) Bull Case Remains
detail:
Jensen Huang Is Back. Nvidia’s (NVDA) Bull Case Remains

NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase

Jensen Huang is back at the helm, and Nvidia's (NVDA) bull case remains in play. Nvidia shares surged 31.5% on November 23 after news of Jensen Huang's reinstatement, underscoring how closely investor confidence in the company is tied to its co-founder.

While near-term volatility is likely to persist, I remain decisively Bullish over the long term. Nvidia makes the chips, networking gear, and software powering the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, and its earnings story is strong enough to ride out the ups and downs.

Huang's Return Restores Continuity, but Not Trust

Huang's return restores strategic continuity, but it does not restore trust overnight. Nvidia disclosed on November 12 that its co-founder and chief executive officer (CEO) had resigned after the board accepted his resignation on November 11. The stock finished that session 4.3% lower. On November 23, Nvidia announced that Huang had been reinstated, and the shares rose 31.5%.

The episode highlighted a degree of key-person risk that I had underestimated. Nvidia's product cadence and customer confidence have always been closely tied to Huang. His return obviously removes the immediate succession problem. However, it leaves investors with a governance question.

The board reinstated him before completing its independent investigation, shortly after creating a National Security and Export Control Committee on November 17 and alongside launching a search for a Chief Compliance Officer. Those oversight steps are the right moves, but they do not excuse reversing a major leadership decision before the facts are settled.

For my Bullish thesis, Huang's return is a stabilizer, though stronger governance is still required.

Nvidia's Earnings Still Point to Powerful AI Demand

Nvidia's results still point to very strong AI demand, and that's the part of the argument I find most compelling. Q3 FY2027 revenue was up 103% year-over-year to $115.8 billion, and Data Center revenue was up 110% to $107.6 billion. GAAP diluted earnings per share (EPS) came in at $2.70. Management has guided to around $130 billion in Q4 FY2027 revenue, plus or minus 3%, all the way through the end of the year, despite assuming zero Data Center compute revenue from China.

Nvidia's product roadmap also gives me confidence the company can sustain growth. The company has started shipping Vera Rubin NVL72, with systems already operating at major cloud partners. This comes as some of its biggest customers continue to invest heavily in AI infrastructure. Meta (META), Google (GOOGL), and Amazon (AMZN) all raised their capital spending plans during their October earnings updates, suggesting that demand for the computing infrastructure Nvidia provides could remain strong.

title: Can Meta's Business Pay For Its Spending?

Can Meta's Business Pay For Its Spending?
Trefis Team

META
Trade META on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Today's big story: Anthropic Broke Its $83 IPO Price. What Did Facebook Do Next?

Meta Platforms is spending on servers, data centers and network infrastructure. Over the last twelve months, its capital spending came to $104 billion. Three years earlier, the twelve-month bill was $28.6 billion. What share of its sales do you think that bill takes now?

How Big Is Meta's Spending Bill?

Over the last twelve months, capital spending took 43.2% of Meta's sales. Three years earlier, it took 22.6%. The bill is now 3.6 times what it was then.

It is still growing. In the quarter to September 2026, spending was 80.3% higher than in the same quarter a year earlier.

Can Meta Pay For It?

In the quarter to September 2026, Meta spent more than its business brought in. The spending took 103.5% of the cash its business brought in. In the same quarter a year earlier, it took 62.8%.

A year earlier, Meta had cash left after the spending in that quarter. This time it had none. It was the only one of the last four quarters below zero.

Meta's spending in the quarter to September was 80.3% higher than a year earlier, and no cash was left after the spending. If much of your savings rides on Meta's share price, you are waiting for that spending to bring in more cash, with little income from Meta meanwhile. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.

Over the last twelve months, the business did cover the bill. The spending took 78.5% of the cash it brought in. But the share jumped in the two latest quarters, to 94.5% in the quarter to June and to more than all of it in the quarter to September.

So in its latest quarter, the business no longer covered the bill. Meta holds $82.4 billion in cash and short-term investments, against $115 billion of debt, counting lease obligations. The cash left over in these figures does not count any cash paid to buy companies. Meta's own measure of free cash flow, which also counts payments on finance leases, was below zero too.

Shares of Alphabet have declined -14.5% over the past year against the Zacks Internet - Services industry's decline of -14.7%. Alphabet's integrated AI stack and growing backlog support returns on infrastructure investment. These positives are offset by rising capital intensity, weaker free cash flow and a larger debt load. Lower monetization of AI Mode queries, advertising concentration and legal remedies create uncertainty around margins.

Meta's shares have declined -5.6% over the past year against the Zacks Internet - Software industry's decline of -7.8%. The company's elevated infrastructure costs are limiting free cash flow, while legal charges add to earnings volatility. Competition for users and advertising budgets remains intense, and Reality Labs continues to incur losses. 

Meta's advertising franchise and liquidity support continued investment, but unproven AI economics, capital efficiency and regulatory exposure keep the long-term risk-reward balanced. Nevertheless, Meta is benefiting from AI-led gains in advertising performance and engagement across its large user base. 

WhatsApp monetization, subscriptions and early Muse adoption expand opportunities beyond traditional advertising. AI glasses also provide another distribution channel for personal agents and services. However, scaling these businesses requires substantial spending before their long-term returns are established.

Further, branch expansion and investments in digital capabilities are expected to strengthen customer engagement, cross-selling opportunities and fee income. 

Despite carrying a substantial debt burden, it maintains a robust liquidity position that will support its capital distributions. Nevertheless, Bank of America's earnings outpaced the Zacks Consensus Estimate in three of the trailing four quarters. 

Elevated expenses from technology investments will likely keep hurting the bottom line. The volatile nature of the capital markets business makes growth in trading revenues uncertain. Weak asset quality is another concern, which might hamper financials.

The Anchor Portfolio agreement provides a cost-plus fee floor, and leasing at Reston Station supports ongoing property services. 

ParkX can sell more services across the managed portfolio and bring in unaffiliated clients, while institutional partnerships can extend Comstock's reach with shared capital. Dependence on affiliates and the Washington, D.C., region remains high. Woodland Pointe and the Oklahoma data-center venture tie up cash, and changes in the value of Jericho securities can obscure operating trends. 

Comstock's undrawn credit line adds a buffer. The rise in recurring fees and operating margins gives the core business room to absorb uneven deal income, with further gains tied to lease-up and the pace of investment spending.

(You can read the full research report on Comstock here >>>)

Shares of Expion Energy have underperformed the Zacks Alternative Energy - Other industry over the past year (-86.1% vs. -27.3%). This microcap company with a market capitalization of $1.95 million has shifted toward higher-margin batteries and away from lower-margin accessories has improved gross profit, with tariff refunds contributing to the gain. Leaner inventories have freed cash, although shortages weighed on sales. 

Expanded Forest River placements, lead-acid battery replacements and upgrades expected in the first half of 2027 could help rebuild sales. The Louisiana prospect offers a second potential revenue source if testing supports commercial production. Financing raised in August lifted cash, but ongoing operating cash burn and planned exploration spending leave Expion reliant on additional funding. 

With sales below year-earlier levels, dependence on a few large customers and exposure to import costs, a sustained recovery requires higher battery volumes and enough capital to fund exploration.

title: Tech Stock Sell-Off: Down 23%, Is Meta a Buy Now?
detail:
Tech Stock Sell-Off: Down 23%, Is Meta a Buy Now?
Patrick Sanders, The Motley Fool

META
NVDA

Trading disclosure

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) has been caught up in the recent tech stock sell-off, with shares down by 23% from their all-time high as investors question whether big tech's massive spending on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure has gotten out of hand.

And Meta is giving investors plenty of reasons to worry. The Facebook and Instagram parent is spending hundreds of billions of dollars on AI infrastructure, with plans to turn what CEO Mark Zuckerberg calls "personal superintelligence" into a new business line.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

But I think this autumn's sell-off, which has brought the stock back to about flat for the past 12 months, also presents an opportunity to invest in one of the "Magnificent Seven" at an attractive price.

Image source: Getty Images.

Meta is spending a fortune on AI

Meta expects capital expenditures (capex) of $135 billion to $145 billion in 2026, more than double the $72 billion it spent last year. Most of that money is going toward data centers and the computing infrastructure needed to develop its Muse AI models.

Meta wants to develop personal AI assistants useful and appealing enough that the company can eventually charge subscriptions for them. It has already introduced paid AI services, but it's too early to know how much revenue they'll produce.

Here's my biggest concern: Unlike Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), and Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Meta Platforms doesn't operate a major cloud computing business that leases out AI computing capacity. That leaves Meta more dependent on its advertising business to finance its enormous investments.

Debt is also becoming an issue.

Meta reported $83.7 billion in total debt at the end of September, compared with $82.4 billion in cash and marketable securities on its books. In addition, Meta has another $420 billion in off-balance-sheet commitments, including future infrastructure obligations, according to a July report from Nikkei Asia.

Those commitments aren't all conventional debt, but they illustrate how much Meta has riding on its AI strategy.

Why Meta stock looks appealing today

For all the concerns about its AI spending, Meta's underlying business is doing extremely well.

In the third quarter, revenue increased by 26% year over year to $64.6 billion, including $63.1 billion in advertising revenue. Ad impressions increased 10%, while the average price per ad climbed 14%.
